## Core Vocabulary

### Basic Greetings
| Spanish | English | Example Sentence | Notes |
|---------|---------|-----------------|-------|
| hola | hello / hi | | Universal, any register |
| buenos días | good morning | | Literally "good days" (plural) |
| buenas tardes | good afternoon | | Used roughly after lunch until dark |
| buenas noches | good evening / good night | | Both greeting and farewell |
| ¿qué tal? | how's it going? | | Informal; often rhetorical |
| ¿cómo estás? | how are you? (informal) | ¿Cómo estás? — Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? | Uses **estar** (temporary state), not ser. Tú form. |
| ¿cómo está usted? | how are you? (formal) | ¿Cómo está usted? — Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y usted? | Usted form — use with strangers, elders, authority. |
| bien | well / good | | |
| muy bien | very well | | |
| más o menos | so-so | | Literally "more or less" |
| regular | okay / not great | | Same word as English, different stress: re-gu-LAR |

### Introductions
| Spanish | English | Example Sentence | Notes |
|---------|---------|-----------------|-------|
| me llamo | my name is (lit. "I call myself") | | Reflexive verb llamarse |
| soy | I am | | From ser — used for identity |
| mucho gusto | nice to meet you | Mucho gusto. — Igualmente. | Literally "much pleasure." Used at first meeting. |
| encantado | delighted to meet you (masc.) | Soy María. — Encantada. | Speaker agrees with own gender: male says **encantado**, female says **encantada**. |
| encantada | delighted to meet you (fem.) | | See above — gender of the speaker, not the listener. |
| igualmente | likewise | | Common reply to mucho gusto |
| ¿cómo te llamas? | what's your name? (informal) | | Tú form |
| ¿de dónde eres? | where are you from? (informal) | | Uses ser — origin is permanent identity |

## Common Collocations
- **mucho gusto en conocerte** — nice to meet you (literally "much pleasure in knowing you"); informal
- **mucho gusto en conocerle** — same, formal (usted)
- **¿a qué te dedicas?** — what do you do for work?; standard introductory question
- **¿de dónde eres?** — where are you from?; always with ser (origin = identity)
- **un placer conocerte** — a pleasure to meet you
- **encantado/a de conocerte** — delighted to meet you

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **presentar** vs **introducir**: "to introduce a person" is **presentar** (Te presento a mi amigo). **Introducir** means "to insert" or "to introduce a topic/concept," not a person.
- **lo siento** vs **perdón**: English "sorry" covers both. **Lo siento** is for genuine regret or sympathy. **Perdón** is for minor social offenses (bumping someone, asking them to repeat).

## Dialect Variations
- **chao**: Standard in most of Latin America. Less common in Spain (which prefers adiós or hasta luego).
- **¿qué onda?**: Mexico and parts of Central America. Extremely informal.
- **¿qué hubo? / ¿quiubo?**: Colombia. Casual greeting, often contracted in speech.
- **tú vs vos**: In Argentina, Uruguay, and parts of Central America, **vos** replaces **tú**. ¿Cómo estás? becomes ¿Cómo estás? (same spelling, different stress in some regions) or ¿Cómo andás?
- **usted usage**: Colombia uses **usted** even among friends and family. Mexico and Spain reserve it for formal situations.

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Cheek-kiss greetings**: One kiss on the cheek is standard in most of Latin America (between women, and between men and women). Two kisses (left-right) in Spain. Men generally shake hands with each other. This applies to introductions and every subsequent greeting.
- **Tú vs usted in introductions**: Default to **usted** with anyone older, in authority, or unknown. In Mexico, strangers often use usted initially, then switch to tú once rapport is established. In Colombia, usted is used even among close friends in some regions.
- **chao**: Despite Italian origin, it is fully standard and not slang in Latin America. Safe to use with anyone you'd address as tú.
- **Buenos días / buenas tardes / buenas noches**: Always used in addition to hola in polite settings. Saying only "hola" to a shopkeeper or elder can feel too casual.
- **Register matters immediately**: Using tú with a stranger in a formal setting (bank, government office) sounds disrespectful. When in doubt, use usted.

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **buenos** — the **ue** is a diphthong: BWEH-nos. Do not separate into two syllables (bu-eh-nos).
- **gracias** — stress on the first syllable: GRA-cias, not gra-CI-as. The **ci** before **a** is a soft "s" sound in Latin America, "th" sound in most of Spain.
- **noches** — the **ch** is always like English "ch" in "church." Stress: NO-ches.
- **llamo** — in most of Latin America, **ll** sounds like English "y" (YA-mo). In Argentina/Uruguay, it sounds like "sh" (SHA-mo). In Spain, varies by region.
- **bien** — one syllable diphthong: BYEN, not "bee-en."
- **disculpe** — stress on second syllable: dis-CUL-pe.
